y collected cube. Milestones get GameAssets.burst(pos, tierColor, 30), and the else branch calls GameAssets.burst(pos) for ordinary cubes. The spec says only milestone counts (1/10/50/100) should fire a GameAssets.burst sparkle. A patched GameAssets.burst saw 101 calls for 101 cash-ins, all with a single argument, so burst fired on every cube including ordinary ones. None of those calls carried the milestone arguments (color, 30), so the milestone case was never distinguished. The checker, which counts milestone-only bursts, therefore found 0 matching calls. I did not establish why `milestone` never evaluated true in my probe; I suspect sentTotal had already advanced past the milestone counts, but I did not check.
Evidence: Probe 7 patched GameAssets.burst and ran 101 CashInService.cashIn calls at one position. It recorded calls=101, every call with args=1. So burst fires for ordinary cubes, and no call carried the 3-argument milestone form (pos, tierColor, 30). The source from probes 5 and 6 shows the unconditional `else GameAssets.burst(burstInfo.part.Position) end` branch for non-milestone cubes.
Fix hint: Call GameAssets.burst only when `milestone` is true, e.g. `if milestone then GameAssets.burst(burstInfo.part.Position, tierColor, 30); burstDone = true end`. For ordinary cubes, drop the GameAssets.burst call and use only the collector's own emitter (`burstInfo.emitter:Emit(8)`). Also confirm sentTotal[player] counts from 1 per player so totals 1, 10, 50 and 100 are hit.

## Lessons from past builds
# Lessons
## Design
- Tune early progression so a playtest of roughly 15 seconds can reach the first purchase or milestone. Use a fast starting income or a cheap first upgrade (a few seconds of income). Slow openings leave the buy loop untested and feel dull. Also keep the second purchase within about 20-30s of idle income, by raising per-item value or lowering the price, so the shop and later upgrades get exercised.
- Do not give starting cash equal to the first upgrade's price. An instant spend gives the player no chase and no sense of what cubes are for. Start slightly below the price so the first few collected cubes earn it, within about 10s.
- The first purchase must actually happen in a short playtest, and its counters (e.g. upgrades_bought) must be above 0. If the report lacks them, the first pad is too hard to find or reach. Put it close to the claimed plot's spawn point, off the walking path, and guide the player to it with a beam. Make sure the tutorial step that points to it fires.
- Give per-event feedback for every economy action: a "+N" popup on collect, plus HUD hints for upgrade cost, affordability or progress. Without it, numbers going up feels weak between purchases.
- Give failure feedback as well as success feedback. A pad or button pressed without enough cash needs a red flash, an audible buzz and a "Need $N" toast, debounced to about 1s. A silent denial confuses young players.
- Place trigger pads (buy pads, claim gates, etc.) off the spawn path so walking from spawn never fires them accidentally. They must still be easy to find and reach: guide the player to the first pad with a visible beam or arrow.
- Make moving cubes or other spawned items non-colliding with players (CanCollide = false, or a collision group) and cap their count per area. Otherwise they jitter, stick or knock players around.
- Keep the time to first core-loop activity well inside the playtest window (the probe may last only ~6-15s). Any auto-claim or auto-start fallback should fire within a few seconds (about 3-5s, not 20s), and claim gates should sit near the spawn area, not far outside the plaza. An idle player must still reach the loop quickly. Keep the spec's auto-claim delay and the tested window consistent so the plaza state can still be observed before the claim.
